scopeNote: Source-paired Tshivenda candidates for the four canonical key points and both quizzes, in source order. keyPoints.sourceEnglish: Balance browns, greens, moisture and air
keyPoints.draft: Linganyisani browns, greens, moisture na air.
keyPoints.literalBacktranslation: Balance browns, greens, moisture and air.
keyPoints.uncertainty: Keeps the source categories at the same scope; removes added dry/fresh qualifiers. Browns, greens, moisture and air remain recognizable compost terms in English.

keyPoints.sourceEnglish: A hot centre does not prove the whole heap is sanitised
keyPoints.draft: Vhukati ho fhisaho a vhu sumbedzi uri heap yoṱhe yo sanitised.
keyPoints.literalBacktranslation: A hot centre does not show that the whole heap has been sanitised.
keyPoints.uncertainty: Retains heap and sanitised in English. The negative evidential claim applies to the whole heap, not only its centre; it does not imply that heat is irrelevant.

keyPoints.sourceEnglish: Keep seed pods and contaminated materials out
keyPoints.draft: Siyani seed pods na contaminated materials nnḓa ha heap.
keyPoints.literalBacktranslation: Keep seed pods and contaminated materials outside the heap.
keyPoints.uncertainty: Retains seed pods and contaminated materials as technical English terms. Heap is supplied from the lesson context so the instruction has a clear object.

keyPoints.sourceEnglish: Judge readiness from the compost condition, not a fixed regional timetable
keyPoints.draft: Ṱolani uri compost yo lugela nga condition yayo; ni songo shumisa fixed regional timetable.
keyPoints.literalBacktranslation: Check whether the compost is ready from its condition; do not use a fixed regional timetable.
keyPoints.uncertainty: Keeps condition and fixed regional timetable in English to avoid implying a specific readiness test or duration. The contrast with judging from compost condition is explicit.

question.sourceEnglish: A farmer's compost heap smells strongly of ammonia and is wet and slimy. What's the fix?
question.draft: Heap ya compost ya mulimi i nukha ammonia nga maanḓa nahone i wet na slimy. Ndi mini zwine zwa nga lugisa?
question.literalBacktranslation: The farmer’s compost heap smells strongly of ammonia and is wet and slimy. What could fix it?
question.uncertainty: Keeps wet in English because the earlier Tshivenda wording could mean raised/high rather than wet. Retains the strong ammonia smell and slimy condition; the request remains a question about a possible fix.

options.draft: Engedzani green material ine ya vha na nitrogen nnzhi

options.sourceEnglish: Add more dry carbon material like straw and turn the heap
options.draft: Engedzani dry carbon material i ngaho straw nahone ni i rembuluse.

options.sourceEnglish: Stop turning it and let it cool
options.draft: Litshani u rembulusa heap, ni i tende i rothole.

options.sourceEnglish: Add more water — the smell means it's too dry
options.draft: Engedzani maḓi manzhi — honoyo munukho u amba uri yo oma nga maanḓa

rationale.sourceEnglish: A wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material. Add dry browns and turn the heap to open it up. An ammonia smell can also suggest too much nitrogen-rich material. Check that the heap stays damp, not soggy.
rationale.draft: A wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material. Engedzani dry browns ni i rembuluse heap to open it up. An ammonia smell can also suggest too much nitrogen-rich material. Check that the heap stays damp, not soggy.
rationale.literalBacktranslation: A wet, slimy heap may need more air and drier material. Add dry browns and turn the heap to open it up. An ammonia smell can also suggest too much nitrogen-rich material. Check that the heap stays damp, not soggy.
rationale.uncertainty: Root retains to open it up English rather than replacing it with air entering; current modal/caution clauses remain exact English. Ordinary add and turn verbs use the independently checked body terminology.

question.sourceEnglish: Why keep wattle seed pods out of an ordinary compost heap?
question.draft: Ndi ngani ni tshi tea u vhea wattle seed pods nnḓa ha ordinary compost heap?
question.literalBacktranslation: Why should you keep wattle seed pods outside an ordinary compost heap?
question.uncertainty: Retains wattle seed pods and ordinary compost heap in English to preserve the exact material and process scope.

options.sourceEnglish: Bark makes every heap too hot
options.draft: Bark i ita uri heap iṅwe na iṅwe i fhise nga maanḓa

options.sourceEnglish: Some seeds may survive and spread when the compost is used
options.draft: Dziṅwe seeds dzi nga survive nahone dza phaḓalala musi compost i tshi shumiswa
Pods dzi kunga termites tshifhinga tshoṱhe

options.sourceEnglish: Pods release a gas that kills every soil organism
options.draft: Pods dzi bvisa gas ine ya vhulaha zwivhumbiwa zwoṱhe zwa soil

rationale.sourceEnglish: An ordinary heap may not expose every seed to conditions that make it non-viable. Excluding pods avoids spreading them with the compost.
rationale.draft: An ordinary heap may not expose every seed to conditions that make it non-viable. U bvisa pods zwi thivhela uri dzi phaḓalale dzi tshi ṱuwa na compost.
rationale.literalBacktranslation: An ordinary heap may not expose every seed to conditions that make it non-viable. Removing pods prevents them from spreading as they go with the compost.
rationale.uncertainty: Root retains the full technical seed-exposure clause as exact English, protecting may not/every seed/conditions/non-viable scope. Ordinary exclusion/spread sentence remains an unreviewed Tshivenda draft.

semanticChecks: Canonical key points, both question strings, every option in order, both rationales, and correct indices [1,1] were checked against current origin/main 3143c07; the packet sourceEnglish fields now match exactly.

The Q0 question retains the strong ammonia smell and wet/slimy state; wet remains English where the prior Tshivenda word was ambiguous. The keyed option adds dry carbon such as straw and turns the heap.

The Q0 rationale preserves may need more air and drier material, dry browns plus turning to open the heap, can also suggest excess nitrogen-rich material, and damp rather than soggy. It makes no definitive diagnosis or guarantee.
Q1 rationale retains may not and every seed, followed by excluding pods to avoid spreading them with compost; it does not claim all seeds survive or an ordinary heap never makes seeds non-viable.
No order, answer index, species, quantities, timing, or sanitation guarantee has been changed.
